etymology: From Old English mete, “food, nourishment,” cognate with the Gothic mats. The narrowing to animal flesh alone is later; in the Authorized Version meat keeps its old, broad sense of any thing eaten.
biblical_def: In the KJV meat is food of any kind, not flesh alone. The modern ear hears meat and thinks of butchered animal — beef, mutton, the roast on the table — but the Authorized Version means whatever nourishes: bread, herbs, milk, fruit, any thing set before a man to be eaten. So at the creation the LORD gave Adam a bloodless table: “Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed... to you it shall be for meat” (Gen 1:29). No flesh is in view there at all, yet it is called meat. Paul reaches for the same word to speak of infancy in the faith: “I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it” (1Co 3:2) — meat here is solid doctrine, the strong food of the mature, set against the milk of first principles. The Psalmist in his passion cries, “They gave me also gall for my meat” (Psa 69:21), a word fulfilled at the cross. And our Lord Himself lifts the term higher than any dish: “My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work” (Joh 4:34). The obedience of the Son was His nourishment. To read meat as flesh only is to starve the word; the AV means the whole provision by which body and soul are fed.
webster_summary: Food of any kind — whatever is eaten for nourishment, not flesh alone.
webster_full: MEAT, food in general; that which is eaten for nourishment, whether herb, grain, fruit, or flesh.
From Old English mete, “food,” the common word for any thing eaten.
The modern narrowing to animal flesh crept in only after the KJV was made.
At creation the herb of the field was given to man for meat (Gen 1:29).
Christ calls the doing of His Father’s will His meat (Joh 4:34).
scriptures: Gen 1:29

And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat.
Joh 4:34
Jesus saith unto them, My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work.
They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.
I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it, neither yet now are ye able.
corruption_summary: No redefinition, only a narrowing of sense: the KJV’s meat is all food, while ours has shrunk to flesh.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here is honest and simple. Where the Authorized Version says meat and means food of every sort, the modern tongue has narrowed the word until it names only flesh. A reader who does not know this will stumble at Gen 1:29, where God gives Adam the seed-bearing herb “for meat,” and will wonder how a plant is called meat at all. He will read Joh 4:34 and imagine our Lord speaking of a dinner rather than of obedience. The remedy is only to restore the old width of the word: meat is what feeds you, be it herb or bread or milk or the strong doctrine of the mature.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that man does not live by bread alone. Scripture uses the word for food precisely to lift the eye past the table: the milk of first principles and the meat of solid teaching (1Co 3:2), the gall given the Sufferer for His meat (Psa 69:21), and above all the meat that never perishes — “My meat is to do the will of him that sent me.” The body is fed with herb and fruit given at creation; the soul is fed with the will of God done and finished. Both are meat, and the second is the greater. To recover the AV sense is to hear the invitation to eat of a bread the world knows nothing of.
roots_summary: Meat means food of any kind, from Old English mete — not flesh only.
roots_lines: Meat — from Old English mete, “food, nourishment.”
In the KJV it means whatever is eaten, herb or grain or flesh alike.
The narrowing to animal flesh is a later English development.
The herb given at creation was man’s first meat (Gen 1:29).
Christ’s meat was to do and finish His Father’s will (Joh 4:34).
usage: “To you it shall be for meat” — the KJV calls the herb of the field meat, for meat is food.
Milk is for babes and meat for the strong: the word means solid doctrine, not a cut of flesh.
The Son’s meat was obedience — a food the world cannot see.

etymology: From Old English rum, “space, extent, opportunity,” cognate with the German Raum. The old sense is open space or a place occupied; the modern sense of a walled chamber is a later specializing of the word.
biblical_def: A room in the KJV is not a chamber with four walls but a place, a position, a seat — the space one occupies at table or in office. The modern reader pictures a room as an enclosed space he walks into; the Authorized Version means the rank he sits in. So our Lord warns, “When thou art bidden of any man to a wedding, sit not down in the highest room” (Luk 14:8) — not the grandest chamber, but the chief seat, the place of honour at the feast. And He bids the guest, “go and sit down in the lowest room” (Luk 14:10), the meanest place, that the host may raise him higher. The word carries the sense of a station one fills: he that occupieth “the room of the unlearned” (1Co 14:16) stands in the place of the ignorant, unable to say Amen to a tongue he cannot understand. Even the nativity turns on it: “there was no room for them in the inn” (Luk 2:7) — no place, no space left, for the Lord of glory. To recover the word is to hear Christ’s parable rightly: it is not about which chamber but about which seat, and beneath the seat, which heart — for he that exalteth himself shall be abased, and the man who takes the lowest room is the one God lifts up.
webster_summary: Space, place, or the seat one occupies — not merely a walled chamber.
webster_full: ROOM, space; place; the seat or position a person occupies at table or in office.
From Old English rum, “space, extent,” akin to German Raum.
The sense of an enclosed chamber is a later narrowing of the broad old word.
The highest room is the chief seat at a feast, not the finest chamber (Luk 14:8).
There was no room — no place — for Christ in the inn (Luk 2:7).
scriptures: Luk 14:8
When thou art bidden of any man to a wedding, sit not down in the highest room; lest a more honourable man than thou be bidden of him;
Luk 2:7
And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.
Else when thou shalt bless with the spirit, how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest?

But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher: then shalt thou have worship in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee.
corruption_summary: No redefinition, only a narrowing: the KJV’s room is a place or seat, while ours has shrunk to a walled chamber.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ear hears room and sees a chamber with a door, and so reads the highest room in Luk 14:8 as the best bedroom rather than the chief seat at the feast. The point of the parable is thereby lost. Christ is not counselling where a man should sleep but where he should sit — how he ranks himself among the guests, whether he grasps at honour or takes the low place. Restore the old sense of room as place and seat, and the whole passage stands upright: the wedding-table, the jostling for precedence, the shame of being told to come down, the joy of being bidden up higher.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the law of the kingdom that the parable teaches: whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased, and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted. The man who chooses the lowest room does not lose by it; he gains, for the Lord of the feast raises him in the sight of all. And behind the table stands the sharper word of Luk 2:7 — that when the King of glory came, there was no room for Him. The world that scrambles for the highest seat could not spare the lowest for its Maker. To take the low room now is to sit where Christ Himself was content to be laid.
roots_summary: Room means space, place, or the seat one occupies — not merely a chamber.
roots_lines: Room — from Old English rum, “space, extent, place.”
In the KJV it means a place or a seat, especially at table.
The highest room is the chief seat; the lowest room, the meanest place.
To occupy the room of the unlearned is to stand in the ignorant man’s place (1Co 14:16).
There was no room — no place — for Christ in the inn (Luk 2:7).
usage: “Sit not down in the highest room” — the KJV’s room is the seat of honour, not a fine chamber.
He took the lowest room, and the host bade him go up higher.
There was no room for them in the inn: no place left for the Lord of glory.

etymology: From the Latin mansio, “a staying, an abiding-place,” from manere, to remain or abide. The word means a dwelling, a resting-place; the modern sense of a large and stately house is a later addition of grandeur.
biblical_def: A mansion in modern speech is a great and stately house, the mark of wealth; but in the KJV it means simply a dwelling, an abode, a resting-place — from the Latin manere, to remain or abide. When our Lord says, “In my Father’s house are many mansions” (Joh 14:2), He is not promising the redeemed a row of palaces, but many abiding-places, room enough in the Father’s house for all His own. The very next breath confirms the sense, for the same abiding is what He offers now: “we will come unto him, and make our abode with him” (Joh 14:23) — abode and mansion are the one word. The dwelling is mutual: He prepares a place for us above, and He takes up His dwelling in us below. Moses knew the deepest mansion of all: “Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations” (Psa 90:1) — God Himself the abode of His people before ever a house was built. And Paul looks past this crumbling tent to the fixed abode to come: “we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2Co 5:1). To read mansion as marble and grandeur is to miss the comfort; the word means a settled, permanent place to abide with God, and that is glory enough.
webster_summary: A dwelling or abiding-place — a place to remain, not a palatial house.
webster_full: MANSION, a dwelling; an abiding-place; the place where one remains or abides.
From Latin mansio, from manere, “to remain, abide.”
The sense of a large and stately house is a later English addition.
In the Father’s house are many mansions — many abiding-places (Joh 14:2).
The same word underlies the abode Christ makes with the believer (Joh 14:23).
scriptures: Joh 14:2
In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you.
Jesus answered and said unto him, If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him.
Psa 90:1
A Prayer of Moses the man of God. Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations.
For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
corruption_summary: No redefinition, only an inflation of the word: the KJV’s mansion is a plain abode, while ours has swelled into a palace.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ear hears mansion and pictures marble, columns, and acreage, and so reads Joh 14:2 as a promise of private palaces in the sky — a heaven of grand estates. But the word in the Authorized Version carries no such swagger; it means an abiding-place, a room to dwell in, from the Latin verb to remain. The many mansions are simply the many resting-places in the Father’s ample house, ready for all His children. Restore the plain sense and the comfort is deeper, not smaller: the promise is not of grandeur but of permanence — a place with the Father that abides.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the mutual indwelling of God and His people. The same word that names our abode above (Joh 14:2) names His abode within us now: “we will come unto him, and make our abode with him” (Joh 14:23). Before ever a house was raised, the LORD Himself was the dwelling-place of His people in all generations (Psa 90:1); and when this earthly tent is dissolved, a building of God, eternal in the heavens, receives us (2Co 5:1). The believer’s true mansion is not a heap of stone but a Person: to abide in Christ, and He in us, world without end.
roots_summary: Mansion means a dwelling or abiding-place, from Latin manere — not a palatial house.
roots_lines: Mansion — from Latin mansio, manere, “to remain, abide.”
In the KJV it means an abiding-place, a dwelling to remain in.
The sense of a stately house is a later English inflation of the word.
The many mansions are many resting-places in the Father’s house (Joh 14:2).
The believer’s mansion is to abide in God, who was ever His people’s dwelling (Psa 90:1).
usage: “In my Father’s house are many mansions” — the KJV means abiding-places, not palaces.
Mansion and abode are the one word: He prepares our dwelling above and makes His dwelling within.
The LORD has been our dwelling place in all generations — the oldest mansion of all.

etymology: From the Latin nepos, “grandson, descendant,” through the Old French neveu. In older English it means a grandson or a descendant generally; the restriction to a brother’s or sister’s son is a later development.
biblical_def: A nephew in the KJV is not a brother’s or sister’s son, as we now use the word, but a grandson — and more broadly a descendant, one of a man’s posterity. The word comes through the Latin nepos, grandson. So Paul charges the church that a widow’s “children or nephews” should “requite their parents” (1Ti 5:4) — her children and grandchildren, the generations she raised, are to care for her in age; piety begins at home and flows down the line and back up it. In judgment the word marks the cutting-off of a whole house: of the wicked it is said, “He shall neither have son nor nephew among his people” (Job 18:19), no child and no grandchild, his name blotted from the earth. So too against Babylon: “I will... cut off from Babylon the name, and remnant, and son, and nephew” (Isa 14:22) — root and branch, seed and seed’s seed. Set against these curses stands the covenant blessing, for “children’s children are the crown of old men” (Pro 17:6). The grandchild is no small thing in Scripture: he is the visible token of a covenant kept to a thousand generations. To read nephew as a sibling’s child is to lose the sweep of the promise — the AV means thy seed after thee, the posterity in whom God shews His faithfulness.
webster_summary: A grandson, or a descendant generally — not a brother’s or sister’s son.
webster_full: NEPHEW, a grandson; and by extension any descendant of the second generation or beyond.
From Latin nepos, “grandson,” through Old French neveu.
The modern restriction to a sibling’s son arose after the KJV was made.
A widow’s nephews are her grandchildren, bound to requite her (1Ti 5:4).
To have neither son nor nephew is to be cut off root and branch (Job 18:19).
scriptures: But if any widow have children or nephews, let them learn first to shew piety at home, and to requite their parents: for that is good and acceptable before God.
He shall neither have son nor nephew among his people, nor any remaining in his dwellings.
For I will rise up against them, saith the LORD of hosts, and cut off from Babylon the name, and remnant, and son, and nephew, saith the LORD.
Pro 17:6
Children's children are the crown of old men; and the glory of children are their fathers.
corruption_summary: No redefinition, only a shift of kinship: the KJV’s nephew is a grandson, while ours is a sibling’s child.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern reader hears nephew and thinks of his brother’s or sister’s boy, and so misreads 1Ti 5:4 as a charge laid on the wider family rather than on the direct line of descent. But the AV means grandson: the widow’s own children’s children, raised in her house, are to requite her in her age. The confusion is easily cleared by the Latin root nepos, grandson, which the older English kept. Read it so, and the passage speaks its plain domestic duty: the generations a mother has poured herself into owe her honour and support when she is old, and to give it is good and acceptable before God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the covenant reach of God’s dealings to a thousand generations — blessing and judgment alike running down the line of seed. To be left “neither son nor nephew” (Job 18:19) is the terror pronounced on the wicked: a name utterly cut off, no grandchild to carry it. To have one’s “son, and nephew” struck from Babylon (Isa 14:22) is judgment to the third generation. But the covenant turns the same reach to mercy: “children’s children are the crown of old men” (Pro 17:6). The grandchild is the visible proof of a promise kept — the LORD showing mercy unto thousands of them that love Him.
roots_summary: Nephew means a grandson or descendant, from Latin nepos — not a sibling’s child.
roots_lines: Nephew — from Latin nepos, “grandson,” via Old French neveu.
In the KJV it means a grandson, or a descendant more broadly.
The modern sense of a sibling’s son is a later narrowing.
A widow’s nephews are her grandchildren, bound to requite her (1Ti 5:4).
Children’s children are the covenant crown of old age (Pro 17:6).
usage: “If any widow have children or nephews” — the KJV means her grandchildren, not her nieces and nephews.
Neither son nor nephew: no child and no grandchild left to keep the name alive.
The nephew of Scripture is a man’s seed after him, the crown of his old age.

etymology: From the Old French passagier, “one who passes,” from passer, to pass. The n crept in as in messenger. It means a passer-by, a traveller on foot; the sense of one carried in a vehicle is modern.
biblical_def: A passenger in the KJV is not one who rides in a conveyance — there were no trains or coaches to ride — but a passer-by, a traveller, one who passes along the way on foot. The modern sense could not exist before the vehicles that made it. So Wisdom lifts her voice in the street “to call passengers who go right on their ways” (Pro 9:15) — the folly of the harlot cries after those passing by, to turn them aside; and Wisdom cries after the same. The word gathers weight in Ezekiel’s vision of the burial of Gog, where the land is so choked with the slain that a valley is named for the travellers: “the valley of the passengers on the east of the sea” (Eze 39:11), and the multitude of corpses shall stop the noses of the passengers. Men are set apart to bury “with the passengers those that remain upon the face of the earth” (Eze 39:14), and every passer-by who “seeth a man’s bone” sets up a sign by it (Eze 39:15). The passenger is simply the man on the road, going by. To read the word as a ticketed rider is anachronism; the AV means the wayfarer, and Scripture makes him a figure of us all — strangers and pilgrims passing through, called at every step to go right on our ways.
webster_summary: A passer-by; a traveller on foot — not one carried in a vehicle.
webster_full: PASSENGER, one who passes by; a traveller on the road; a wayfarer.
From Old French passagier, from passer, “to pass.”
The intruding n matches the like change in messenger and harbinger.
The sense of a rider carried in a coach or train is wholly modern.
Wisdom calls to the passengers who go right on their ways (Pro 9:15).
scriptures: Pro 9:15
To call passengers who go right on their ways:

And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will give unto Gog a place there of graves in Israel, the valley of the passengers on the east of the sea: and it shall stop the noses of the passengers: and there shall they bury Gog and all his multitude: and they shall call it The valley of Hamongog.

And they shall sever out men of continual employment, passing through the land to bury with the passengers those that remain upon the face of the earth, to cleanse it: after the end of seven months shall they search.
And the passengers that pass through the land, when any seeth a man's bone, then shall he set up a sign by it, till the buriers have buried it in the valley of Hamongog.
corruption_summary: No redefinition, only anachronism: the KJV’s passenger walks by on the road, while ours is carried in a vehicle.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ear hears passenger and sees a rider on a bus or plane, a ticketed traveller carried along. But no such thing existed when the word was set in Pro 9:15; the passenger there is a passer-by on foot, one who goes right on his way through the street where both Wisdom and Folly cry after him. The very phrase “who go right on their ways” shows he is walking, not being carried. Restore the plain sense — a passer-by, a wayfarer — and Ezekiel’s grim valley reads clearly too: the travellers who pass through the land, so many of them that a valley of graves is named for them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the believer himself is a passenger in the old sense — a stranger and pilgrim passing through, with no continuing city here. The street of Pro 9 is a parable of the whole life: Folly sits at her door and calls the passer-by to turn in and die, and Wisdom lifts her voice to the same travellers to keep them in the way. Every man on the road is bidden two ways at once. To recover the word is to feel the summons of the pilgrimage: we do not dwell here; we are passing by, and the great question is whose voice we heed as we go right on our ways.
roots_summary: Passenger means a passer-by or traveller on foot, from passer — not a carried rider.
roots_lines: Passenger — from Old French passagier, passer, “to pass.”
In the KJV it means a passer-by, a traveller on the road.
The intrusive n matches messenger and harbinger.
The sense of a carried rider is wholly modern.
Wisdom and Folly both cry after the passengers going by (Pro 9:15).
usage: “To call passengers who go right on their ways” — the KJV’s passenger walks by, he is not carried.
The valley of the passengers is named for the travellers passing through, not for riders.
The believer is a passenger in the old sense: a stranger and pilgrim passing by.

etymology: From the Old French cariage, “that which is carried,” from carier, to carry. In the KJV it means baggage, goods, the load one bears; the sense of a wheeled vehicle for persons is a later English development.
biblical_def: A carriage in the KJV is never a wheeled vehicle for persons — that sense came centuries later — but that which is carried: baggage, goods, burdens, the gear an army or traveller bears. It is carriage in the plain old sense, the thing you carry. So when David went to face Goliath, “David left his carriage in the hand of the keeper of the carriage, and ran into the army, and came and saluted his brethren” (1Sa 17:22) — he laid down his baggage to run light into the battle. Luke uses it of Paul’s company: “we took up our carriages, and went up to Jerusalem” (Act 21:15), gathering up their bundles for the road. Isaiah sees the Assyrian laying up his stores as he advances: “at Michmash he hath laid up his carriages” (Isa 10:28). And the Danites “put the little ones and the cattle and the carriage before them” (Jdg 18:21), their whole moveable substance driven ahead. In every place the word means the load, not the coach. To recover it is to see David’s faith the plainer: he set down all he carried and trusted an empty hand and the name of the LORD of hosts. The pilgrim travels light; he lays his carriage in the Keeper’s hand and runs to the field.
webster_summary: That which is carried; baggage or goods — not a wheeled vehicle for persons.
webster_full: CARRIAGE, that which is carried; baggage, goods, burdens borne on a journey or to war.
From Old French cariage, from carier, “to carry.”
The sense of a coach or wheeled vehicle for persons is a later development.
David left his carriage — his baggage — to run into the battle (1Sa 17:22).
Paul’s company took up their carriages and went up to Jerusalem (Act 21:15).
scriptures: And David left his carriage in the hand of the keeper of the carriage, and ran into the army, and came and saluted his brethren.
And after those days we took up our carriages, and went up to Jerusalem.
He is come to Aiath, he is passed to Migron; at Michmash he hath laid up his carriages:
So they turned and departed, and put the little ones and the cattle and the carriage before them.
corruption_summary: No redefinition, only a shift of thing: the KJV’s carriage is the baggage carried, while ours is the vehicle that carries.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ear hears carriage and sees a coach drawn by horses, or a railway car — a thing that carries people. But the AV means the very opposite end of the act: the thing that is carried. David’s carriage in 1Sa 17:22 is not a chariot he rode but the baggage he set down and left with the keeper. A reader who does not know this pictures David dismounting from a coach on a battlefield of foot-soldiers, which is nonsense. Restore the old sense — carriage is load, baggage, goods — and the scene stands: a boy lays aside all he was carrying and runs empty-handed to the fight.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the readiness of faith to lay every burden down. David left his carriage in the hand of the keeper and ran into the army; he would not go weighed down into the LORD’s battle. The pilgrim travels light, and the soldier of Christ entangles himself with no encumbrance. There is a Keeper into whose hand every burden may be committed: casting all your care upon Him, for He careth for you. To recover the word is to feel the summons to run unladen — to set down what we carry, that with an empty hand and a full heart we may run toward the field where the name of the LORD of hosts wins the day.
roots_summary: Carriage means that which is carried, baggage, from carier — not a vehicle.
roots_lines: Carriage — from Old French cariage, carier, “to carry.”
In the KJV it means baggage, goods, the load borne on a journey.
The sense of a coach or wheeled vehicle is a later development.
David left his carriage — his baggage — to run into the battle (1Sa 17:22).
The soldier of Christ lays down every carriage that would weigh him down.
usage: “David left his carriage in the hand of the keeper” — the KJV means his baggage, not a coach.
They took up their carriages: they shouldered their bundles for the road.
Lay your carriage in the Keeper’s hand and run light into the LORD’s battle.

etymology: From the Old French porchacier, “to seek eagerly, to procure,” from por- (forth) and chacier, to chase. The root sense is to pursue and obtain; the narrowing to buying with money is a later specializing.
biblical_def: To purchase in the KJV is not narrowly to buy with coin, but broadly to acquire, to gain, to obtain — to get for oneself by whatever means, price or blood or labour. The word is wider than a shop transaction. So Judas “purchased a field with the reward of iniquity” (Act 1:18) — gained it, procured it, by his betrayal. A faithful deacon does not buy but earns: “they that have used the office of a deacon well purchase to themselves a good degree” (1Ti 3:13), obtaining a good standing and great boldness in the faith. Above every earthly acquiring stands the great purchase of the gospel, and here the price is named: the Holy Ghost has made overseers to feed “the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28). Christ did not haggle for His people; He bought them outright, and the coin was His own life poured out. They are His purchased possession, and the Spirit within them is the earnest of it “until the redemption of the purchased possession, unto the praise of his glory” (Eph 1:14). To read purchase as mere buying is to shrink it; the AV means to obtain and to own — and the church’s comfort is that she was obtained at the dearest price, and is owned by Him who paid it.
webster_summary: To acquire, gain, or obtain by any means — not merely to buy with money.
webster_full: PURCHASE, to acquire; to gain; to procure or obtain, by price, labour, or any means.
From Old French porchacier, “to pursue, procure,” from chacier, to chase.
The narrowing to buying with money is a later specializing of the word.
A faithful deacon purchases — obtains — a good degree (1Ti 3:13).
Christ purchased the church with His own blood (Act 20:28).
scriptures: Act 1:18
Now this man purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
For they that have used the office of a deacon well purchase to themselves a good degree, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Eph 1:14
Which is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession, unto the praise of his glory.
corruption_summary: No redefinition, only a narrowing: the KJV’s purchase is to obtain by any means, while ours has shrunk to buying with money.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ear hears purchase and thinks only of a shop, a price, coins across a counter. But the AV word is far wider: to purchase is to procure, to acquire, to obtain by whatever means. A deacon who serves well is said to purchase a good degree (1Ti 3:13), though no money changes hands; he gains it by faithful labour. Judas purchased a field, but the reward was the wage of iniquity, not an honest price. Restore the breadth of the word, and the great texts open: the church is not something Christ shopped for, but a possession He obtained — and the means He used to obtain it was His own blood.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the costly, effectual purchase of redemption. “The church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28) is no bargain and no negotiation, but an outright buying at the dearest price ever paid. His people are the purchased possession, already His by right of blood, and the Spirit given them is the earnest, the down-payment guaranteeing the full redemption to come (Eph 1:14). This is the anchor of assurance: the redeemed did not purchase themselves, nor were they cheaply had. They were obtained by the Son at the cost of His life, and what He has purchased He will surely keep unto the praise of His glory.
roots_summary: Purchase means to acquire, gain, or obtain by any means — not merely to buy.
roots_lines: Purchase — from Old French porchacier, “to pursue, procure.”
In the KJV it means to acquire or obtain, not narrowly to buy.
A deacon purchases a good degree by faithful service, not by coin (1Ti 3:13).
Christ purchased the church with His own blood (Act 20:28).
The saints are His purchased possession, sealed by the Spirit’s earnest (Eph 1:14).
usage: “Purchase to themselves a good degree” — the deacon obtains it, though no money is paid.
Christ purchased the church with His own blood: He obtained her at the dearest price.
The Spirit is the earnest of the purchased possession, until the redemption is complete.

etymology: From the Latin scientia, “knowledge,” from scire, to know. In the KJV it means simply knowledge or learning; the modern sense of an organized empirical method for mastering nature is wholly later.
biblical_def: Science in the KJV is simply knowledge — from the Latin scientia, from scire, to know. It carries none of our modern freight of laboratories, method, or the mastery of nature; it means what is known, learning, understanding. So Daniel and his fellows were chosen as youths “skilful in all wisdom, and cunning in knowledge, and understanding science” (Dan 1:4) — men of understanding and learning, fit to stand in the king’s palace. And Paul, closing his charge to Timothy, sets a warning over the word that the modern age has forgotten: “keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called” (1Ti 6:20). There is a knowledge that is no knowledge, a learning that sets itself against the truth of God — science falsely so called. The apostle knew the danger of a wisdom that puffs up and opposes: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men... and not after Christ” (Col 2:8). All true knowing begins in another place than the schools suppose: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Pro 1:7). To read science as our word is to miss both the breadth of the term and the sharpness of Paul’s warning: not all that names itself knowledge is knowledge indeed.
webster_summary: Knowledge or learning in general — that which is known, not the modern empirical method.
webster_full: SCIENCE, knowledge; learning; that which is known or may be known.
From Latin scientia, from scire, “to know.”
The modern sense of an organized empirical method for mastering nature is wholly later.
Daniel and his fellows were skilful in wisdom and understanding science (Dan 1:4).
Paul warns against oppositions of science falsely so called (1Ti 6:20).
scriptures: O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
Dan 1:4

Children in whom was no blemish, but well favoured, and skilful in all wisdom, and cunning in knowledge, and understanding science, and such as had ability in them to stand in the king's palace, and whom they might teach the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Pro 1:7
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
corruption_summary: The word once meaning all knowledge has been captured by scientism, which absolutizes empirical method as the only knowledge there is.
corruption_paragraphs: Here a real corruption has grown up around the word, and it must be named. In the KJV science is knowledge of every kind — Daniel’s learning, the understanding fit to stand in a king’s palace (Dan 1:4). But the modern age has narrowed the word to empirical, measurable inquiry, and then, worse, has absolutized that one narrowed thing. Scientism is the creed that only what can be weighed, counted, and repeated in a laboratory counts as knowledge at all — that theology, morality, and the testimony of God are mere opinion, while science alone gives fact. This is not science; it is a philosophy about science, smuggled in under the prestige of the lab coat. It cannot be proved by its own method, for the claim “only empirical knowledge is real” is not itself an empirical finding. It is faith — faith in the sufficiency of the creature’s measuring-rod.

Paul answered it before it was born. “Avoiding... oppositions of science falsely so called” (1Ti 6:20): there is a thing that wears the name of knowledge and opposes the truth, and it is to be shunned, not courted. “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit... after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ” (Col 2:8). The rudiments of the world dressed in modern authority are still the rudiments of the world. The believer honours true knowledge — the LORD gave men minds to search out His works — but he denies that the measuring of matter is the whole of knowing. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Pro 1:7). Every real science begins there, or it is science falsely so called.
roots_summary: Science means knowledge or learning, from Latin scire, “to know” — not the modern method.
roots_lines: Science — from Latin scientia, scire, “to know.”
In the KJV it means knowledge or learning of any kind.
The modern empirical sense — and scientism’s worship of it — is wholly later.
Daniel understood science: he was a man of deep learning (Dan 1:4).
There is a science falsely so called, to be shunned, not courted (1Ti 6:20).
usage: “Understanding science” — the KJV means Daniel was learned, not that he ran experiments.
Paul warns against science falsely so called: knowledge that opposes the truth of God.
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge — every true science starts there.

etymology: From the Anglo-French several, from Medieval Latin separalis, akin to separare, to sever or separate. The root sense is separate, distinct, belonging to each apart; the vaguer modern sense of “a few” is a later weakening.
biblical_def: Several in the KJV does not mean “a few, more than two,” as we now use it, but separate, individual, distinct — each one apart, belonging to itself. It comes from the same root as sever, to divide. So the leprous king Uzziah “dwelt in a several house” (2Ki 15:5) — not one of several houses, but a separate house, cut off by himself in his uncleanness. In the parable the lord gives to his servants talents “to every man according to his several ability” (Mat 25:15) — the distinct, particular measure proper to each. The offerings likewise are reckoned one by one: “a several tenth deal of flour” (Num 28:13) is a separate portion for each lamb. And the great doctrine of the gifts turns on this sense, for the Spirit divideth “to every man severally as he will” (1Co 12:11) — not by the crowd but one by one, particularly, sovereignly. To read several as a vague handful is to blur a precise word. The AV means each apart, each distinct: the leper in his own house, the servant with his own measure, the saint with his own gift — and behind every several portion, the one Spirit who apportions to each as He will.
webster_summary: Separate, distinct, individual — each apart by itself, not merely “a few.”
webster_full: SEVERAL, separate; distinct; individual; belonging to each one apart.
From Anglo-French several, akin to Latin separare, “to sever, separate.”
It shares its root with sever, to divide or set apart.
The weakened modern sense of “a few” is a later development.
Uzziah dwelt in a several — a separate — house in his leprosy (2Ki 15:5).
scriptures: And the LORD smote the king, so that he was a leper unto the day of his death, and dwelt in a several house. And Jotham the king's son was over the house, judging the people of the land.
And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey.
But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will.
And a several tenth deal of flour mingled with oil for a meat offering unto one lamb; for a burnt offering of a sweet savour, a sacrifice made by fire unto the LORD.
corruption_summary: No redefinition, only a weakening: the KJV’s several means separate and distinct, while ours has faded to “a few.”
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ear hears several and counts “a small handful, more than two,” and so misreads 2Ki 15:5 as though Uzziah lived in one of several houses. But the word means separate: he dwelt in a several house because his leprosy set him apart, shut off from the palace and the people. So too “several ability” in the parable (Mat 25:15) is not a plural quantity of ability but each servant’s own distinct measure. Restore the old sense — separate, particular, each apart — and every text sharpens: the leper apart in his house, the servant with his own proper trust, the lamb with its own several portion of flour.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the particular, individual dealing of God with each of His own. The Spirit divides “to every man severally as he will” (1Co 12:11): not a general shower on the crowd, but a distinct gift measured out one by one, sovereignly, to each saint. The Master gives talents “according to his several ability” (Mat 25:15) — He fits the trust to the man, and will reckon with each apart. This is both comfort and summons: no believer is lost in the mass, for the LORD knows and portions to each severally; and none may bury his one talent because another has five. Each must answer for his own several trust.
roots_summary: Several means separate, distinct, individual — each apart, not merely “a few.”
roots_lines: Several — akin to Latin separare, “to sever, separate.”
In the KJV it means separate, distinct, belonging to each apart.
It shares its root with sever, to divide.
Uzziah dwelt in a several — separate — house (2Ki 15:5).
The Spirit divides to every man severally, each apart, as He will (1Co 12:11).
usage: “He dwelt in a several house” — the KJV means a separate house, not one of several.
To every man his several ability: each servant’s own distinct measure.
The Spirit gives severally, apportioning to each saint his own particular gift.

etymology: From the Old French vil, “cheap, of low value,” from the Latin vilis, of small price. The first sense is lowly, worthless, held cheap; the sense of morally foul is a strengthening that later crowded out the plainer meaning.
biblical_def: Vile in modern speech means morally foul, disgusting, wicked; but in the KJV its first sense is far plainer — of no esteem, lowly, worthless, held cheap. It is the opposite of honourable, not always the opposite of holy. So Paul speaks of the body we now carry, not as sinful in itself, but as lowly and mean: Christ “shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body” (Php 3:21) — our body of humiliation, this weak and dying frame, raised and glorified. James warns the church against judging by esteem, when a rich man in a gold ring is fawned upon and “there come in also a poor man in vile raiment” (Jas 2:2) — cheap, shabby clothing, of no account in the world’s eyes. The word can carry the fuller weight of contempt earned by sin, as when Eli’s sons “made themselves vile” (1Sa 3:13), or when Daniel foresees that “a vile person” shall stand up and obtain the kingdom by flatteries (Dan 11:21). Both senses meet: what the world counts vile, God often exalts; what exalts itself, God counts vile. To read the word only as wicked is to lose the comfort of Php 3:21 — the vile body is not the sinful body but the lowly one, and it shall be made glorious.
webster_summary: Of no esteem; lowly, cheap, worthless — not always morally wicked.
webster_full: VILE, of no esteem or value; lowly; cheap; worthless; held in low account.
From Old French vil, from Latin vilis, “of small price.”
The first sense is low or cheap; the sense of morally foul is a later strengthening.
Our vile body is our lowly body, to be changed to glory (Php 3:21).
The poor man’s vile raiment is his cheap and shabby clothing (Jas 2:2).
scriptures: Php 3:21
Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself.
Jas 2:2
For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment;
For I have told him that I will judge his house for ever for the iniquity which he knoweth; because his sons made themselves vile, and he restrained them not.
And in his estate shall stand up a vile person, to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom: but he shall come in peaceably, and obtain the kingdom by flatteries.
corruption_summary: No redefinition, only a strengthening: the KJV’s vile means lowly and of no esteem, while ours has hardened to “wicked.”
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ear hears vile and thinks only of the morally revolting, and so reads Php 3:21 as though our present body were a filthy, sinful thing to be got rid of. But the word there means lowly — of no esteem, cheap, humble — not corrupt. The body that shall be changed is not our wickedness but our weakness: this mortal, aching, dying frame, held in low account, which Christ will fashion like unto His glorious body. Restore the plainer sense and the comfort returns: the vile body is the humble body, and its low estate is not its doom but the very thing that shall be swallowed up in glory.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the great reversal of esteem that runs through Scripture. What the world counts vile, God delights to exalt: the poor man in vile raiment, despised in the assembly (Jas 2:2), is chosen rich in faith; the lowly body, held cheap, is raised in glory (Php 3:21). And what the world crowns, God counts vile: “a vile person” obtains the kingdom by flatteries (Dan 11:21), and Eli’s sons “made themselves vile” and were judged (1Sa 3:13). The word thus holds both estates in one hand. The believer need not fear to be reckoned vile by men, for the LORD lifts the lowly; and he must fear to be vile before God, which is another and a dreadful thing.
roots_summary: Vile means of no esteem, lowly, cheap, from Latin vilis — not always “wicked.”
roots_lines: Vile — from Latin vilis, “of small price, cheap.”
In the KJV its first sense is lowly, worthless, of no esteem.
The hardening to “morally foul” is a later strengthening of the word.
Our vile body is our lowly body, to be changed to glory (Php 3:21).
What the world counts vile, God exalts; what exalts itself, God counts vile.
usage: “Our vile body” — the KJV means our lowly, humble body, not our sinful one.
The poor man came in vile raiment: cheap and shabby, despised by the rich.
A vile person by the world’s flatteries won a crown — and was vile before God.
